doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: Oral tradition, teaching and Shiny Stockings
title: Teaching feeling in schools and Ruth Brown
summary: Hughes says Foster teaches feeling to student bands at Hampton; talk turns to Ruth Brown and the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis album.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You know you’re saying something here that I think is very rich. You know what you just said right now, the first thing, the response that it got from me and Monk is it made us laugh, because of the insight of it, you know the insight that you give the male/female thing, the call and response thing. Every time you talk about call and response I think of a choir and a preacher, you know? But the other thing I was saying is see so little of this is taught in schools.

That’s one thing that Frank has been trying to do with this band is to go into schools and tell people how the thing was really done — not from a, well I won’t say an educational standpoint, but from —

Yeah not from that theoretical standpoint but from the feeling standpoint. And we’ve been, well we have this particular thing that we do at Hampton University where all these little bands come in and they play their thing and Frank and a few of the other guys critique these bands. And they particularly hone in on the feeling that the kids are getting. Because that’s the one thing that they do miss. I mean they’re getting all this stuff in the schools but they don’t get the basic, you’ve got to have a feeling to play this thing. You know, let’s start to express ourselves, the way we feel. Not only what the notes are saying, but how you feel about those notes, you know? And we’d like to spread that around more, but it doesn’t happen as often as we’d like.
I think there’s a big part of teaching that’s sometimes left out is just dealing with hearing and playing something from in here where, instead of off a sheet of paper.

You know Ruth? We were talking with Ruth and basically what she said was when you play these notes, these notes are expensive. The notes cost you something. You know there’s an emotional price tag to those notes.
You can’t put it any better than that. And if anybody knows, she knows, cause you can hear her giving it out again.
She told us some stories about traveling that were, something else.
And she did an album with one of the greatest jazz bands in the history of this country as far as I was concerned, was the Thad Jones - Mel Lewis Band. And she did an album that was just killing.
It really was. It still is.
